rv.q: Soldiers of Tomorrow emerges as an illuminating, embracing hour of political theatre nonetheless.
There are some shortcomings, but it’s not every day you get a thoughtful ex-IDF soldier ruminating on his experiences at length.
In the end, Soldiers of Tomorrow may prove a little too reflective to convincingly grapple with the big questions it raises, let alone suggest any answers.
As a personal meditation on how institutional systems challenge individual morality, it works brilliantly.
Engaging in a moral debate that goes beyond the Israeli-Arab dichotomy, this is a sobering meditation.

The result is certainly fascinating, and I found that time flew by, Erdal's storytelling and Anita Rochon's direction ensuring that there was always enough variety, whether or not you agreed with what he was saying!
This excellent show is directed by Anita Rochon, with designer Brian Ball and artist Juliette Demoulin’s colourful set, which suggests the great sweep of Judea, or is it Palestine?
It’s performed with a bright, ringing confidence by de Nordwall that suggests it certainly means something to her but it fails to communicate much more than a lingering sense of befuddlement.

cn.t: Erdal's personal monologue about his IDF service tackles the Israeli-Palestinian conflict with warmth and wit, though some find it theatrically unsharpened. Critics praise its nuanced, softly-delivered storytelling, even as the show sparks controversy outside the theater.
